report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .34", "p = .12", "p = .61"), Sentence = c("No significant results were found for gender (b = -.25, SE = .26, p = .34) or age (b = -.09, SE = .06, p = .12) with regards to the overall grade.", "No significant results were found for gender (b = -.25, SE = .26, p = .34) or age (b = -.09, SE = .06, p = .12) with regards to the overall grade.", "Girls provided a higher rating of the app's appearance than boys (b = .06, SE = .25, p = .01) but no effects were found for age (b = -.03, SE = .06, p = .61)." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. text.text: Background: Over 17% of children live with a chronic somatic illness and are at increased risk of experiencing psychological problems, such as anxiety and depression.
Grow It!

is a transdiagnostic mobile health (mHealth) intervention that combines experience sampling and personalised mood feedback with daily coping challenges to promote reflection, emotional insight and adaptive coping.
The app fosters a collaborative team experience in which participants contribute to growing a shared virtual tree and communicate through a chat function with predesigned stickers.
Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the acceptability of the Grow It!
app among adolescents with a chronic somatic illness and to identify key lessons the development of other gamified mHealth apps designed to promote well-being.
Methods: This preregistered study is part of a randomised waitlist controlled trial.
Adolescents with a chronic somatic illness aged 10-18 years old were recruited from a university medical children's hospital.
Upon inclusion, adolescents were randomised to an intervention group that used the Grow It!
app or a waitlist control group.
Follow up questionnaires were completed immediately after the four week intervention period and three months later.
Consecutively, the waitlist control group was also offered the Grow It!
app and completed questionnaires immediately after use and three months later.
Participants completed user experience survey comprising open ended and closed questions after playing the app.
Responses were analysed using qualitative content analysis and descriptive statistics.
Results: Between August 2021 and September 2023, 208 adolescents were included in the study.
Due to participant attrition, the user experience survey was distributed to 183 participants and completed by 150 (Mage=13.95, 39.33% male, 59.33% female, 1.33% other).
The app received a mean overall rating of 7.32 out of 10, and a mean look-and-feel rating of 7.98 out of 10; 84% would recommend the app to a friend.
Participants reported that the app helped them recognise their emotions and gain greater self-insight.
They also described its design as colourful and visually appealing.
Suggested improvements included adjusting the timing and frequency of the momentary assessments, and expanding the chat function to allow free-text messages or a wider selection of stickers.
The Grow It!
app is well-accepted by adolescents aged 10 to 18 with a chronic somatic illness, although optimising the chat function and reducing questionnaire burden may further improve user experience.
Combined with evidence of effectiveness, these findings on acceptability and user experience support the implementation of the Grow It!
app in paediatric healthcare.

text.text: The Grow It!

The app targets three working mechanisms: 1) emotional awareness, through daily emotion diary questionnaires using the Experience Sampling Method (ESM), 2) emotion reflection, through a personalised mood profile reflecting the ESM outcomes, and 3) enhancing adaptive coping, through daily challenges based on Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT).

Rather than focussing on specific implementation outcomes, the survey focussed on the overall experience and experience of different components of the app.

The survey contained three sections, which map onto our three research questions: 1) Overall rating of the app and look and feel, 2) rating of the psychological working mechanisms (evaluation of ESM, evaluation of challenges in the app, evaluation of the mood profile), and What grade would you rate the appearance of the app?").
The survey consisted of 24 questions.
The full (translated) version is available in the preregistration [28].

text.text: Quantitative data were summarised using descriptive statistics.
Means and standard deviations were calculated for all quantitative data.
Hierarchical regression analyses were conducted to assess whether age, gender and medical diagnoses were related to the overall grade of the app and the grade of the look and feel.
To assess significance of these two-sided tests, p-values were compared to α = .05.
Multiple testing was corrected for using the procedure for False Discovery Rates (FDR) described by Benjamini and Hochberg [30].
text.formatted: Multiple testing was corrected for using the procedure for False Discovery Rates (FDR) described by Benjamini and Hochberg <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Qualitative data were analysed using inductive content analysis on a manifest level.
First, the survey responses were read by two researchers (MvD and a research assistant), after which initial codes were developed independently by the two researchers based on 25 surveys.
In a first consensus meeting, the codes were discussed and code sheets were developed.
The code sheets were used by the researchers to code the first 25 surveys, after which they were discussed in a consensus meeting.
The intercoder-reliability was 89.47%.
After this each researcher coded half of the remaining data.
All data analysis scripts and raw output are available on the OSF [31].
text.formatted: All data analysis scripts and raw output are available on the OSF <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Initially, we set out to determine whether the participants' medical diagnosis would 222 influence ratings on the app.
This data was self-reported by participants.
As the quality of this 223 data was not sufficient to reliably determine the diagnosis, the diagnosis was not used in the 224 regression analyses.
A total of 208 adolescents were randomised into the intervention group (n = 105) or 227 control group (n = 103).
Due to participant drop-out, the user experience survey was 228 distributed to 183 participants and completed by 150 (81.97%).

text.text: Most responses related to participants perceiving the app as being colourful and/or attractive (35.33%) or as just nice (18.56%).
As one participant highlighted: "It was very colourful and child friendly, and this way I really wanted to do a challenge or complete questionnaires each day." (female, 17 years old).
Other positive responses related to clear instructions in the app (10.18%) and good game mechanics (5.99%).

A small portion of responses were negative and related to perceiving the lay-out as boring (6.59%) or childish (4.19%), with one participant saying "It looked nice, but more for young children, not really for teenagers." (female, 17 years old).

When asked whether the Grow It!

However, most participants said the app helped them only a little (46.67%).

For participants offering an additional explanation, they often mentioned that they were already coping well: "I am someone with a positive outlook and I'm not really impacted by my disease" (male, 10 years old).
When asked to elaborate on how the app helped them, most participants reported that they were better at recognising emotions (32.58%), as shown in Figure 4.

text.text: Most responses (21.48%) related to an altruistic, intrinsic motivation to want to participate in research.

However, a large group of participants seemed to be motivated by extrinsic factors such as a financial motivation (11.41%), other people motivating them (10.74%) or due to habit (7.38%), mostly due to the prompts on their phone.

Some participants were motivated both by intrinsic and extrinsic factors, as this participant elaborated on why she wanted to participate in the study: "To get to know myself better and mainly to help you [the researchers]" (female, 15 years old).
Research question 2 focused on the acceptability of the psychological working mechanisms in the Grow It!
app.
The first psychological working mechanism was emotional awareness, targeted through ESM mood questionnaires.
These were sent out five times a day.
The majority of participants (69.33%) reported that these questions had some effect on them.
On a multiple choice question, the most often reported effect of the ESM questions was thinking about how participants felt (46.67%) or getting to know oneself better (26.67%).
A minority (6.67%) reported that the questions made them feel better.
At the same time, the frequency of the questions was perceived as too high by about half of the participants (51.33%).
The second working mechanism was reflection on emotions, targeted through the mood profile.
This mood profile provided feedback to the participants, based on their answers to the ESM questions.
Most participants thought the way information was displayed in the mood profile was very clear (35.33%) or totally clear (24%).

About half of the participants (49.33%) indicated that the mood profile had an effect on them, such as making them think about how they feel more often (26.67%) or getting to know themselves better (18.67%).
The other half of the participants (50.67%) felt they were not affected by the mood profile.
About a quarter of the participants (22%) indicated that they shared their mood profile with others (e.g., parents, teachers or healthcare professionals).
The third psychological working mechanism was adaptive coping, targeted through CBT-based challenges.
The majority of the participants (55.33%) thought this had no effect on them.
For the participants that did indicate an effect, they most often reported that they were more physically active (15.33%) or that they were better at accepting situations (14%).
The third research question focused on wants and needs for further development.
Results of suggestions for improvements are shown in Figure 6.

For the participants that did suggest changes, most suggestions were related to the questionnaires and the chat function.

This study investigated the acceptability of the Grow It!
app, a multiplayer mHealth app that aims to promote mental well-being, through emotional awareness, reflection on emotions and adaptive coping [20].
text.formatted: app, a multiplayer mHealth app that aims to promote mental well-being, through emotional awareness, reflection on emotions and adaptive coping <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: In a series of iterations with game-designers, youth and healthcare professionals, this app was developed to meet the unique needs of adolescents with a chronic somatic illness.
A total of 150 Dutch youth aged 10 to 18 with a chronic illness played the Grow It!
app for four weeks and completed a user experience survey.

This provided us with the first insights into the acceptability of the overall look and feel, the acceptability of the psychological working mechanisms and adolescents´ wants and needs for further development.
Results showed that the Grow It!
app was acceptable in terms of overall rating and look and feel.
More specifically, a total of 84% would recommend the app to their friends, which is 10% higher than results on Grow It!
in the general population [20].
text.formatted: in the general population <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>.

text.text: The overall acceptability of the app did not depend on the participants' age or gender, while the appearance was rated somewhat higher by girls.
This suggests that the app can be widely implemented, but that the design and appearance could be improved for boys.
Combined with evidence for effectiveness, the app is recommended for adolescents with mild psychological complaints [26].
text.formatted: Combined with evidence for effectiveness, the app is recommended for adolescents with mild psychological complaints <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: Despite good ratings of the overall look and feel, almost half of the participants thought the app did not help them or did little to help them.
This is also corroborated in the quantitative findings described in the main outcome paper of the study [26], where we did not find an overall group effect of the Grow It!
text.formatted: This is also corroborated in the quantitative findings described in the main outcome paper of the study <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>, where we did not find an overall group effect of the Grow It!

text.text: app when compared to a waitlist control group.
Instead, results in that paper highlighted that the app may be especially effective for adolescents with pre-existing symptoms of anxiety and depression.
These results may in part be explained by the sample selection.
All participants received high-quality care and (psychosocial) support from the hospital, leading to a sample with very little symptoms of anxiety and depression.
In addition, participants may be differentially impacted by their medical diagnosis.
For instance, participants with a cleft will typically visit the hospital every few years, possibly leading to a lesser impact of their medical diagnosis.
Teams were created to increase competition and enhance learning [32].
text.formatted: Teams were created to increase competition and enhance learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">[32]</ref>.

text.text: In this study, the team aspect of the game was appreciated by participants when asked broadly about their overall experience.
However, follow-up questions highlighted that the way of communicating with the team (i.e., through a closed chat using stickers only) was not rated as well as the overall team experience.
In addition, many of the suggested changes related to the chat function.
The Grow It!
app does not allow free input of text in the chat due to privacy and safety concerns.

This seems to contradict the needs and wants of youth, of whom some indicated they wanted an open chat or wanted more stickers, highlighting an important tradeoff between facilitating contact, while taking privacy and safety concerns into account.
The app seemed appropriate to use and seemed to help participants in recognising their emotions or helping to get to know themselves better.
This could be due to the regular ESM questions and the feedback provided with the mood profile.
In in-depth interviews with participants of the Grow It!
study, their parents and healthcare professionals also showed that the app fostered emotional awareness and early recognition of emotional difficulties [33].
text.formatted: study, their parents and healthcare professionals also showed that the app fostered emotional awareness and early recognition of emotional difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref>.

text.text: Other studies have shown that completing ESM questions can lower depressive symptoms [34] and that participants may adjust their mood based on feedback using ESM outcomes [35].
text.formatted: Other studies have shown that completing ESM questions can lower depressive symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> and that participants may adjust their mood based on feedback using ESM outcomes <ref type="bibr">[35]</ref>.

text.text: The mood profile provided a real-time overview of the participants' current and past mood.

This psychological working mechanism was perceived as clear, with about half of the participants reporting some effect of the mood profile, such as recognising their emotions better or getting to know themselves better.
However, despite the current results, results from Grow It!
in the general population show that adding the mood profile did not change the overall compliance nor did it improve psychological outcomes [29].
text.formatted: in the general population show that adding the mood profile did not change the overall compliance nor did it improve psychological outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref>.

text.text: In addition, the overall rating for the app in the general population also remained unchanged after introducing the mood profile in the app.
It remains unclear how the mood profile in its current form contributes to changes in mental well-being.
Similar to the mood profile, about half of the participants did not think the challenges had an effect on them.
Interestingly, the challenges were not named by participants as something that needed to be changed about the Grow It!
app.

Although CBT has been proven to be an effective element of mHealth apps [15], the challenges in its current form do not seem to be related to mental health outcomes when measured both qualitatively and quantitatively [26].
text.formatted: Although CBT has been proven to be an effective element of mHealth apps <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>, the challenges in its current form do not seem to be related to mental health outcomes when measured both qualitatively and quantitatively <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>.

text.text: It is possible that the goal of the challenges is unclear to participants.
The app does not contain an explanation of why participants should do the challenges, or what coping technique the challenges target.
Including psychoeducational feedback on coping can potentially improve participant experience and app effectiveness [6].
text.formatted: Including psychoeducational feedback on coping can potentially improve participant experience and app effectiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: Some participants were motivated by intrinsic factors, such as wanting to test a new app, but the majority were motivated by extrinsic factors, such as the possibility of winning a prize.
Clearly, participants' motivation for taking part in research differs from the motivation of patients in an outpatient hospital clinic.
This is especially important when implementing mHealth apps [36], as research results may not translate directly into clinical practice.
text.formatted: This is especially important when implementing mHealth apps <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[36]</ref>, as research results may not translate directly into clinical practice.

text.text: Professionals developing or working with mHealth apps should take this difference into account, by also conducting real-world implementation studies [36, 37].
text.formatted: Professionals developing or working with mHealth apps should take this difference into account, by also conducting real-world implementation studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">[36,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">37]</ref>.

text.text: Participants provided many helpful suggestions for next design iterations.
Suggestions for improvements were primarily related to the ESM questionnaires.
In research settings, participants are typically given multiple-item questionnaires multiple times per day [21].
text.formatted: In research settings, participants are typically given multiple-item questionnaires multiple times per day <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">[21]</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, these questionnaires may increase participant burden [38].
text.formatted: At the same time, these questionnaires may increase participant burden <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">[38]</ref>.

text.text: Although we used gamification elements where participants could earn points for completing the questionnaires, the sampling scheme was not personalised or tailored to participants' schedules, possibly influencing their motivation and compliance.
For instance, participants wanted a different timing or a longer time window during which they could complete the ESM questionnaires.
As such, as next development step could include more tailoring options for participants by adding their own questions or providing the possibility of changing the ESM schedule.
Another next step is to focus on the multiplayer experience.
Although participants quite liked to play in a team, the chat function was suboptimal.
Data on Grow It!
from the general population also showed that the team element can be experienced as frustrating when other team members are not actively earning points towards the team tree [25].
text.formatted: from the general population also showed that the team element can be experienced as frustrating when other team members are not actively earning points towards the team tree <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">[25]</ref>.

text.text: From an implementation perspective, team-based participation is less feasible as eight participants must register for the Grow It!
app before the team can start.
This creates a waiting period between registration and participation.
Therefore, another development step is to change the multiplayer experience.
Players will play individually and grow their own tree, and are able to see other players' trees in order to feel part of a community and are motivated to grow their tree.
To maintain the social experience, players will be able to send predefined supportive messages to other players.
This study assessed the acceptability of one of the first mHealth apps for youth with a chronic illness.
A strength of this study is that both quantitative and qualitative data were combined to study acceptability.
Second, we were able to include a sample with a wide age range and representative gender distribution.
One specific challenge we encountered, was measuring mental well-being during school hours, as not all participants were allowed to use their phone during school hours.
This highlights an important conflict between obtaining ecologically valid measurements for researchers on the one hand and feasibility for the participants on the other hand.

The feasibility for participants can be improved, for instance, by providing them with letters for their school, detailing why the school should allow the participant to use their phone during the intervention period.
Another option for implementation in clinical practice would be to personalise the sampling schemes to better tailor towards adolescent's specific time schedules and preferences [e.g., 39].
Another limitation is that a selection bias may have influenced the results.
Approximately 20% of participants randomised into the study did not complete the user experience survey.
Participants who stopped using the app prematurely may have been less likely to complete the user experience survey, potentially resulting in their experiences being underrepresented in the findings.
In addition, youth who were less inclined to use mHealth apps may have been less likely to participate in the study in the first place.
However, it is unclear to what extent this bias would generalise to a healthcare setting.
It is possible that mHealth apps do not appeal to all adolescents for reasons that are not necessarily related to the quality or acceptability of the app itself.
For example, some youth may prefer face-to-face contact over using digital applications altogether [40] and may thus refrain from using mHealth apps such as Grow It!.
text.formatted: For example, some youth may prefer face-to-face contact over using digital applications altogether <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">[40]</ref> and may thus refrain from using mHealth apps such as Grow It!.

text.text: In conclusion, results showed that the Grow It!
app was acceptable to youth with a chronic somatic illness.
Participants appreciated the look and feel, and psychological working mechanisms.
However, important considerations remain.

For instance, the ESM questionnaires could be more personalised toward adolescents' needs, psychoeducation can be included to explain the purpose of the psychological working mechanisms and the social experience of the app can be improved.
Combined with evidence of effectiveness [26], we learned that it is acceptable, appropriate and potentially effective to use the Grow It!
text.formatted: Combined with evidence of effectiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>, we learned that it is acceptable, appropriate and potentially effective to use the Grow It!

text.text: app in paediatric healthcare.
However, real-world studies should be conducted to understand how Grow It!
can be successfully implemented into paediatric healthcare.
